proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(n\ge 12\), \(h\in(0,r_0]\), \(k\ge1\), and the two positive integer pilot dimensions.  Then \(m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor\ge4\), so the ordered quadratic average in \(\mathrm{def{:}private\text{-}higher\text{-}order\text{-}learner}\) is well defined.  The privacy domain specified there is
\[
 \mathcal O_0=[0,1]^d\times\{0,1\}\times[0,1].
\]
This is also the almost-sure support of an observed record under every \(Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{att}}\): by \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\),
\[
 Y=A Y(1)+(1-A)Y(0),
\]
and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcomes}\) makes the right-hand side an element of \([0,1]\) almost surely.  The differential-privacy argument below in fact holds on all of \(\mathcal O_0^n\), independently of the data-generating law.

First fix realizations of the two projected pilots \((\bar\pi,\bar\mu)\).  If the projection sets in \(\mathrm{def{:}private\text{-}higher\text{-}order\text{-}learner}\) are nonempty, membership of the projections in those sets gives the pointwise bounds below.  If a set is empty, the prescribed fallback gives the same bounds because \(0<\kappa<1/2\).  Thus in every case
\[
 \kappa\le \bar\pi(x)\le1-\kappa,
 \qquad 0\le\bar\mu(x)\le1
 \quad (x\in\mathcal X).
\]
Consequently, for \(o=(x,a,y)\in\mathcal O_0\), every scalar factor among
\[
 a,\quad a-\bar\pi(x),\quad a\{a-\bar\pi(x)\},
 \quad y-\bar\mu(x)
\]
has absolute value at most one.  The same assertion holds for the primed record.  Write \(c_\rho\) and \(c_b\) for the deterministic basis constants in the construction.  Since \(K_h(x)\le h^{-d}\), and since Euclidean vectorization preserves the Frobenius norm, the two components of the linear kernel satisfy
\[
 \|\operatorname{vec}L_Q(o)\|_2\le c_\rho^2h^{-d},
 \qquad
 \|L_R(o)\|_2\le c_\rho h^{-d}.
\]
It follows, with \(c_L=(c_\rho^4+c_\rho^2)^{1/2}\), that
\[
 \|L(o)\|_2\le c_Lh^{-d}.
\]
For the quadratic kernel, Cauchy--Schwarz and the stated normalization of \(b_{h,k}\) give, whenever both basis factors can be nonzero,
\[
 \left|b_{h,k}(x)^{\mathsf T}b_{h,k}(x')\right|
 \le \|b_{h,k}(x)\|_2\|b_{h,k}(x')\|_2
 \le c_b^2 k h^{-d}.
\]
If either factor is off \(C_h\), the inner product is zero by the support condition on \(b_{h,k}\), so this bound remains valid globally.  Hence
\[
 \|\operatorname{vec}H_Q(o,o')\|_2
 \le c_b^2c_\rho^2 k h^{-2d},
 \qquad
 \|H_R(o,o')\|_2
 \le c_b^2c_\rho k h^{-2d}.
\]
Thus, for \(c_H=c_b^2(c_\rho^4+c_\rho^2)^{1/2}\), the deterministic clipping radii in the construction obey
\[
 \Lambda_L\le c_Lh^{-d},
 \qquad
 \Lambda_H\le c_Hkh^{-2d}.
\]
These inequalities are uniform over every admissible value of the projected pilots and hence over \(Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{att}}\).

Consider two replacement-adjacent main-block samples \(D_*\) and \(D_*'\), differing only at index \(r\).  Every clipped linear summand has norm at most \(\Lambda_L\), so the difference of the two linear averages has norm at most \(2\Lambda_L/m\).  In the ordered quadratic sum, precisely the \(2(m-1)\) ordered pairs \((r,j)\) and \((j,r)\), \(j\ne r\), can change.  Every clipped quadratic summand has norm at most \(\Lambda_H\), and therefore the difference between its old and new values has norm at most \(2\Lambda_H\).  The triangle inequality now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|T_*(D_*)-T_*(D_*')\|_2
 &\le {2\Lambda_L\over m}
   +{2(m-1)\,2\Lambda_H\over m(m-1)}\\
 &= {2\Lambda_L+4\Lambda_H\over m}\\
 &\le {C_\Delta\over m}\{h^{-d}+kh^{-2d}\},
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
 C_\Delta=\max\{2c_L,4c_H\}.
\]
This is a deterministic conditional sensitivity bound.  Its constant depends only on \((d,\kappa,\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) and the fixed basis normalizations (indeed the displayed choice only uses their constants), as required.

We next verify every Gaussian calibration.  For \(u\in\{\pi,\mu\}\), replacement of one record in its pilot block changes the unnoised average by
\[
 \left\|{1\over m}\sum_{i=1}^m z_u(O_i)
      -{1\over m}\sum_{i=1}^m z_u(O_i')\right\|_2
 ={1\over m}\|z_u(o)-z_u(o')\|_2
 \le\Delta_u
\]
by the definition of \(\Delta_u\).  The supremum is finite because the fixed finite-dimensional tensor-spline coordinates are bounded on the compact cube and \((a,y)\in\{0,1\}\times[0,1]\).  The preceding main-block calculation shows in the same way that \(\overline\Delta_*=(2\Lambda_L+4\Lambda_H)/m\) is a valid replacement sensitivity bound conditional on the pilots.

The symbol assumptions give \(0<\epsilon_n\le1\) and \(0<\delta_n<1/2\).  Therefore
\[
 0<\epsilon_n^\circ=\min\{\epsilon_n,1/2\}<1,
 \qquad
 c_{\delta_n}=\sqrt{2\log(1.25/\delta_n)}+1
 >\sqrt{2\log(1.25/\delta_n)}.
\]
Applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}gaussian\text{-}mechanism\text{-}replacement}\) to each pilot average proves that each pilot release is \((\epsilon_n^\circ,\delta_n)\)-differentially private on its own block.  Conditional on any fixed pilot realization, applying the same lemma to \(T_*\) and \(\overline\Delta_*\) proves that the main release is \((\epsilon_n^\circ,\delta_n)\)-differentially private on \(D_*\).

It remains to show that the adaptive use of the pilots does not add the three budgets.  Denote the two pilot releases by \(Z_\pi^{\mathrm{rel}},Z_\mu^{\mathrm{rel}}\) and the main release by \(W^{\mathrm{rel}}\), and consider the full internal transcript
\[
 \mathcal T=(Z_\pi^{\mathrm{rel}},Z_\mu^{\mathrm{rel}},W^{\mathrm{rel}}).
\]
If adjacent full samples differ in \(D_*\), the joint law \(\nu\) of the pilot releases is unchanged.  For any measurable transcript event \(E\), let \(E_z\) be its section at pilot value \(z\), and let \(K_D(z,\cdot)\) be the conditional law of the main release.  Conditional main-block privacy gives
\[
 K_D(z,E_z)\le e^{\epsilon_n^\circ}K_{D'}(z,E_z)+\delta_n
 \quad\text{for every }z.
\]
Integration against the common law \(\nu\) gives
\[
 \Pr_D(\mathcal T\in E)
 \le e^{\epsilon_n^\circ}\Pr_{D'}(\mathcal T\in E)+\delta_n.
\]

If the changed record lies in \(D_\pi\), condition on the unchanged blocks \((D_\mu,D_*)\).  Once \(Z_\pi^{\mathrm{rel}}=z\) is fixed, drawing \(Z_\mu^{\mathrm{rel}}\), constructing both projected pilots, and drawing the main release defines a Markov kernel \(K(z,\cdot)\) that is identical for the two adjacent values of \(D_\pi\).  For a measurable transcript event \(E\), put \(g(z)=K(z,E)\in[0,1]\).  The event form of pilot privacy also controls bounded measurable functions: by the layer-cake identity and the privacy inequality for each set \(\{g>t\}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \int g\,d\mathsf P_D
 &=\int_0^1\mathsf P_D\{g>t\}\,dt\\
 &\le\int_0^1
   \left(e^{\epsilon_n^\circ}\mathsf P_{D'}\{g>t\}+\delta_n\right)dt\\
 &=e^{\epsilon_n^\circ}\int g\,d\mathsf P_{D'}+\delta_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is exactly the privacy inequality for the full transcript.  The argument for a replacement in \(D_\mu\) is identical.  If the replaced record is among the at most two discarded observations, the transcript is unchanged.  These four exhaustive cases prove adaptive parallel composition:
\[
 \mathcal T\text{ is replacement }(\epsilon_n^\circ,\delta_n)\text{-differentially private}.
\]
Because \(\epsilon_n^\circ\le\epsilon_n\), monotonicity of the defining inequality in its first parameter makes \(\mathcal T\) replacement \((\epsilon_n,\delta_n)\)-differentially private.

Finally, reconstruction of the pilot functions, metric projection, spectral flooring, matrix inversion, and evaluation at \(x_0\) are measurable functions of the transcript and public tuning parameters.  For any such measurable map \(F\) and event \(B\), applying the transcript privacy inequality to \(F^{-1}(B)\) proves the same privacy inequality for \(F(\mathcal T)\).  Thus the returned \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}(x_0;h,k)\), and hence \(\mathsf M_{h,k,J_\pi,J_\mu}^{\mathrm{DP}}\), are \((\epsilon_n,\delta_n)\)-differentially private.  The radius in \(\mathrm{def{:}private\text{-}confidence\text{-}interval}\) is deterministic given the public parameters, and interval formation and intersection with \([-1,1]\) are further measurable post-processing.  Therefore \(C_n(h,k)\) has the same replacement privacy guarantee.

Put
\[
 \ell=hk^{-1/d},\qquad
 r_o=n^{-1/(2+d/\gamma)},\qquad
 r_2=n^{-1/\{1+d/(2\gamma)+d/(2q)\}},
\]
and let
\[
 t=r_{\mathrm{up}}
   =r_{\mathrm{np}}\vee r_{\mathrm{reg}}\vee r_{\mathrm{ho}}.
\]
We first reduce the three envelopes to a form convenient for tuning.  The constraints
\(1\le k\le mh^d\) imply
\[
 m^{-1/d}\le \ell\le h\le r_0\le 1/4.
\]
Since \(n\ge12\) and \(m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor\),
\[
 n/4\le m\le n/3.
\]
Consequently, Definitions \(\mathrm{def{:}bias\text{-}envelope}\),
\(\mathrm{def{:}sampling\text{-}envelope}\), and
\(\mathrm{def{:}privacy\text{-}envelope}\), together with
\(\sqrt{a+b}\le\sqrt a+\sqrt b\) for \(a,b\ge0\), give a constant
\(C<\infty\), depending only on the fixed class constants and \(\eta\), such that
\[
 B(h,k)
 =C_B\{h^\gamma+\ell^q+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha\}
 \le C\{h^\gamma+\ell^q\},                                      \tag{1}
\]
where the last inequality uses \(\ell\le1\) and \(\alpha>0\),
\[
\begin{split}
 S(h,k,\eta)
 &\le C\left\{n^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}
       +n^{-1}h^{-d/2}\ell^{-d/2}\right\},                       \tag{2}
\end{split}
\]
where \(k^{1/2}=h^{d/2}\ell^{-d/2}\), and
\[
 G(h,k,\eta,\epsilon_n,\delta_n)
 \le C N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}
       \{h^{-d}+h^{-d}\ell^{-d}\}.                               \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, the four terms of the corrected sampling envelope are covered by
\(M_h=mh^d\ge k\ge1\): after absorbing the fixed powers of
\(x_\eta=\log(8/\eta)\), its square-root term is bounded by the two terms on
the right of (2), its \(M_h^{-1}\) term is bounded by \(M_h^{-1/2}\), its
\(k^{1/2}M_h^{-3/2}\) term is bounded by \(k^{1/2}M_h^{-1}\), and its
\(kM_h^{-2}\) term is the square of \(k^{1/2}M_h^{-1}\), which is at most
\(k^{1/2}M_h^{-1}\).  Replacing \(m\) by \(n\) within fixed factors then gives
(2).  For (3), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}phase\text{-}rate}\) gives
\[
 N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}
 ={\sqrt{\log(1/\delta_n)\log(1/\eta)}\over n\epsilon_n},
\]
while the ratio between the logarithmic factor in the privacy envelope and the
one in this display is
\(\sqrt{\log(8/\eta)/\log(1/\eta)}\); also \(n/m\le4\).
Thus the constant in (3) is uniform in \(n,\epsilon_n,\delta_n\).

We next rewrite the privacy-free rate.  Since \(s=q/2\), the first branch in
Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}phase\text{-}rate}\) is \(r_2\), and its branch
condition is
\[
 q<{d\over2\{1+d/(2\gamma)\}}.                                   \tag{4}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 1+{d\over2\gamma}+{d\over2q}>2+{d\over\gamma}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 q<{d\over2\{1+d/(2\gamma)\}}.
\]
Because \(n>1\), this comparison of denominators proves, including equality at
the boundary in (4), that
\[
 r_{\mathrm{np}}=r_o\vee r_2.                                    \tag{5}
\]

We construct a feasible comparison pair \((h,k)\).  All constants used in this
construction are fixed independently of \(n,\epsilon_n,\delta_n\).  First
suppose \(q<\gamma\).  With
\[
 a_q={1\over1+d/\gamma+d/q},
\]
the corrected definition has \(r_{\mathrm{ho}}=N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-a_q}\).
The restrictions \(\epsilon_n\le1\) and \(\delta_n<1/2\) imply
\[
 N_{\mathrm{priv}}
 \le {n\over\sqrt{\log 2\,\log(1/\eta)}}=:C_\eta n.              \tag{6}
\]
As \(a_q\le q/d\), equations (6) and \(t\ge r_{\mathrm{ho}}\) imply
\[
 t^{1/q}\ge C_1 n^{-1/d}\ge C_2m^{-1/d}                         \tag{7}
\]
for positive constants \(C_1,C_2\).  Choose a fixed \(A\ge C_2^{-1}\), and set
\[
 h=t^{1/\gamma},\qquad \ell_0=A t^{1/q},\qquad
 k=\left\lfloor (h/\ell_0)^d\right\rfloor.                       \tag{8}
\]
There is a fixed \(t_0\in(0,1)\) such that, whenever \(t<t_0\),
the inequality \(q<\gamma\) makes \(\ell_0\le h\), so \(k\ge1\).
Equation (7) and the choice of \(A\) give
\[
 k\le(h/\ell_0)^d\le mh^d.                                      \tag{9}
\]
If \(K=(h/\ell_0)^d\ge1\), then
\(\lfloor K\rfloor\ge K/2\).  Hence the actual value
\(\ell=hk^{-1/d}\) satisfies
\[
 \ell_0\le\ell\le2^{1/d}\ell_0.                                \tag{10}
\]
Integer rounding therefore changes every ensuing bound by only a fixed factor.

The four fluctuation inequalities required in (2)--(3) follow directly from
the four components of \(t\).  Indeed, by (5),
\[
\begin{split}
 t\ge r_o
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n^{-1/2}t^{-d/(2\gamma)}\le t,\\
 t\ge r_2
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n^{-1}t^{-d/(2\gamma)-d/(2q)}\le t.                              \tag{11}
\end{split}
\]
Also, because
\(r_{\mathrm{reg}}=N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1/(1+d/\gamma)}\) and
\(r_{\mathrm{ho}}=N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1/(1+d/\gamma+d/q)}\),
\[
\begin{split}
 t\ge r_{\mathrm{reg}}
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}t^{-d/\gamma}\le t,\\
 t\ge r_{\mathrm{ho}}
 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}t^{-d/\gamma-d/q}\le t.                  \tag{12}
\end{split}
\]
Substitution of (8)--(12) into (1)--(3) yields
\[
 B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)+G(h,k,\eta,\epsilon_n,\delta_n)\le C t.      \tag{13}
\]
The remaining feasibility requirements also hold uniformly for all sufficiently
large \(n\).  In fact, \(t\ge r_o\) gives
\[
 mh^d=mt^{d/\gamma}
 \ge {1\over4}n^{\,2\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\longrightarrow\infty,    \tag{14}
\]
so (14) eventually implies
\(mh^d\ge C_S^2\log(8/\eta)\).  By decreasing \(t_0\), if necessary,
we also have \(h\le r_0\).  Equations (9) and (14) now verify every stated
constraint.

Suppose instead that \(q\ge\gamma\).  For \(t<t_0\), take
\[
 k=1,\qquad h=t^{1/\gamma},\qquad \ell=h.                         \tag{15}
\]
Then \(h^q\le h^\gamma=t\).  The first term in (2) is at most \(Ct\)
by \(t\ge r_o\).  The second term in (2) is
\[
 n^{-1}h^{-d}
 =\{n^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}\}^2\le t^2\le t.                            \tag{16}
\]
Here \(\bar q=\gamma\), so the corrected definition gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{ho}}
 =N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1/(1+2d/\gamma)}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}h^{-2d}\le t,                             \tag{17}
\]
and, since \(h\le1\), (17) also bounds
\(N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-1}h^{-d}\).  Equations (1)--(3) and
(15)--(17) again prove (13).  Feasibility follows from (14), now with \(k=1\),
and from \(h\le r_0\).  This calculation also identifies the two advertised
privacy regimes: (12) is the \(q\)-branch when \(q<\gamma\), whereas (17) is
the private-Gram rate \(N_{\mathrm{priv}}^{-\gamma/(\gamma+2d)}\)
when \(q\ge\gamma\).

It remains to justify minimization and the case in which the rate is not small.
For all sufficiently large \(n\), \((h,k)=(r_0,1)\) is feasible, so the feasible
set is nonempty.  For each feasible integer \(k\), its admissible bandwidths
form a closed subinterval of \((0,r_0]\), bounded away from zero by
\[
 h\ge\max\left\{(k/m)^{1/d},
 \{C_S^2\log(8/\eta)/m\}^{1/d}\right\}.
\]
There are only finitely many possible integers \(k\le mr_0^d\), and the objective
is continuous in \(h\) on each such interval.  Hence a deterministic minimizer
exists, after any fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule.  When \(t<t_0\), its
objective is no larger than (13).  When \(t\ge t_0\), Definition
\(\mathrm{def{:}private\text{-}confidence\text{-}interval}\) gives
\(C_n(h,k)\subseteq[-1,1]\), and therefore
\[
 \operatorname{length}\{C_n(h,k)\}\le2\le (2/t_0)t.              \tag{18}
\]
When \(t<t_0\), the same definition and nonnegativity of the three envelopes give
\[
 \operatorname{length}\{C_n(h,k)\}
 \le2R_n(h,k)
 =2\{B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)+G(h,k,\eta,\epsilon_n,\delta_n)\}
 \le2Ct.                                                          \tag{19}
\]
The bounds (18)--(19) are pointwise in the realized sample and do not involve
the pilot dimensions \(J_\pi,J_\mu\).  Taking expectation under each
\(Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{att}}\) and then the supremum over that class proves
the asserted inequality with \(C_L=\max\{2C,2/t_0\}\).  All lower bounds on
\(n\) used in feasibility depend only on the fixed class constants and \(\eta\),
which yields the stated \(n_0\).

Fix \(\eta\in(0,1/4)\) and all structural constants, and let the constants implicit in \(\lesssim\), \(\gtrsim\), and \(\asymp\) be independent of \(n\) but allowed to depend on those fixed quantities.  Put
\[
 x_\eta=\log(8/\eta),\qquad
 \mathcal D_n=\left\{(h,k):0<h\le r_0,\ k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\ k\le mh^d,\ mh^d\ge C_S^2x_\eta\right\}.
\]
For \((h,k)\in\mathcal D_n\), define the proof intermediates
\[
 \ell=hk^{-1/d},\qquad M=mh^d,\qquad
 a=M^{-1/2},\qquad b=\frac{\sqrt{k}}{M}
     =m^{-1}h^{-d/2}\ell^{-d/2}.
\]
The definitions of \(B\) and \(S\) give the exact identities
\[
 B(h,k)=C_B\{h^\gamma+\ell^q+h^\gamma\ell^\alpha\}
\]
and
\[
 S(h,k,\eta)=C_S\left\{
 \sqrt{x_\eta(a^2+b^2)}+x_\eta a^2+x_\eta^{3/2}ab+x_\eta^2b^2
 \right\}.
\]
Indeed, \(M^{-1}+kM^{-2}=a^2+b^2\), \(\sqrt{k}M^{-3/2}=ab\), and \(kM^{-2}=b^2\).  Since \(C_B,C_S>0\), \(x_\eta>0\), and \(\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\ge(a+b)/\sqrt2\), there is a constant \(c>0\) such that every admissible pair satisfies
\[
 B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)
 \ge c\{h^\gamma+\ell^q+a+b\}.
 \tag{1}
\]

We first prove the lower bound.  The rank constraint \(k\le mh^d\) implies
\[
 \ell=hk^{-1/d}\ge m^{-1/d}\ge n^{-1/d},
\]
where the last inequality uses \(m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor\le n\).  Hence (1) yields
\[
 B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)\gtrsim n^{-q/d}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Define
\[
 r_o=n^{-1/(2+d/\gamma)},\qquad
 r_2=n^{-1/\{1+d/(2\gamma)+d/(2q)\}},\qquad
 A_*=\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac d{2q}.
\]
If \(h^\gamma<r_o\), then, using \(m\le n\),
\[
 a=m^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}
 \ge n^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}
 >n^{-1/2}r_o^{-d/(2\gamma)}=r_o.
\]
If instead \(h^\gamma\ge r_o\), the first term already has this size.  Thus (1) implies
\[
 B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)\gtrsim r_o.
 \tag{3}
\]
Likewise, unless either \(h^\gamma\ge r_2\) or \(\ell^q\ge r_2\), one has
\[
 b=m^{-1}h^{-d/2}\ell^{-d/2}
 \ge n^{-1}h^{-d/2}\ell^{-d/2}
 >n^{-1}r_2^{-A_*}=r_2.
\]
Consequently (1) also gives
\[
 B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)\gtrsim r_2.
 \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2)--(4), followed by taking the infimum over \(\mathcal D_n\), prove
\[
 \inf_{(h,k)\in\mathcal D_n}\{B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)\}
 \gtrsim r_o\vee r_2\vee n^{-q/d}.
 \tag{5}
\]

We next identify the privacy-free rate in this display.  Since \(s=q/2\), the low-smoothness condition in the definition of \(r_{\mathrm{np}}\) is equivalent to
\[
 q<\frac{d}{2\{1+d/(2\gamma)\}}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 1+\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac d{2q}>2+\frac d\gamma
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 q<\frac{d}{2\{1+d/(2\gamma)\}}.
\]
Because \(n>1\), this says that \(r_2>r_o\) exactly in the low-smoothness branch; at equality the two rates coincide, and in the remaining branch \(r_o\ge r_2\).  Therefore the piecewise definition of the phase rate gives
\[
 r_{\mathrm{np}}=r_o\vee r_2.
 \tag{6}
\]

For the matching upper bound, set
\[
 T=r_o\vee r_2\vee n^{-q/d}.
\]
All three powers have positive exponents, so \(T\to0\).  The definitions of \(r_o\) and \(r_2\), together with \(T\ge r_o\vee r_2\), imply
\[
 n^{-1/2}T^{-d/(2\gamma)}\le T,
 \qquad
 n^{-1}T^{-A_*}\le T.
 \tag{7}
\]
For \(n\ge12\), \(m=\lfloor n/3\rfloor\ge n/4\).

Suppose first that \(q\ge\gamma\).  Choose
\[
 h=T^{1/\gamma},\quad k=1,\quad \ell=h.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(h\le r_0\), and
\[
 M=mh^d\ge \frac n4 r_o^{d/\gamma}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus eventually \(k\le M\) and \(M\ge C_S^2x_\eta\), so this choice belongs to \(\mathcal D_n\).  Since eventually \(h\le1\), the bias definition and \(q\ge\gamma\), \(\alpha>0\), give
\[
 B(h,1)=C_B\{h^\gamma+h^q+h^{\gamma+\alpha}\}\lesssim T.
\]
Also, by (7),
\[
 a=m^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}\le2n^{-1/2}T^{-d/(2\gamma)}\le2T,
 \qquad b=M^{-1}=a^2\lesssim T,
\]
where the last bound uses \(T\le1\) eventually.  Substitution in the exact display for \(S\) above shows \(S(h,1,\eta)\lesssim T\).

Now suppose that \(0<q<\gamma\).  Put
\[
 h=T^{1/\gamma},\qquad
 \widetilde\ell=4^{1/d}T^{1/q},\qquad
 K=(h/\widetilde\ell)^d.
\]
Because \(1/\gamma-1/q<0\) and \(T\to0\), one has \(K\to\infty\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\), set \(k=\lfloor K\rfloor\).  Then \(K\ge2\), so
\[
 \frac K2\le k\le K,
 \qquad
 \widetilde\ell\le \ell=hk^{-1/d}\le2^{1/d}\widetilde\ell.
 \tag{8}
\]
The floor term in \(T\) and the bound \(m\ge n/4\) imply
\[
 \widetilde\ell
 =4^{1/d}T^{1/q}
 \ge4^{1/d}n^{-1/d}
 \ge m^{-1/d}.
\]
Hence \(K\le mh^d=M\), and therefore \(1\le k\le M\).  As in the preceding case,
\[
 M\ge \frac n4 r_o^{d/\gamma}\longrightarrow\infty,
\]
so eventually \(h\le r_0\), \(M\ge C_S^2x_\eta\), and the rounded pair lies in \(\mathcal D_n\).  By (8), and because \(\ell\le1\) eventually,
\[
 h^\gamma=T,
 \qquad
 \ell^q\le 8^{q/d}T,
 \qquad
 h^\gamma\ell^\alpha\le T;
\]
thus \(B(h,k)\lesssim T\).  Finally, (7), (8), and \(m\ge n/4\) yield
\[
 a=m^{-1/2}h^{-d/2}\le2n^{-1/2}T^{-d/(2\gamma)}\le2T
\]
and
\[
 b=m^{-1}h^{-d/2}\ell^{-d/2}
 \le4n^{-1}T^{-d/(2\gamma)}\widetilde\ell^{-d/2}
 =2n^{-1}T^{-A_*}\le2T.
\]
The exact formula for \(S\) now gives
\[
 S(h,k,\eta)
 \le C_S\left\{\sqrt{x_\eta}(a+b)+x_\eta a^2+x_\eta^{3/2}ab+x_\eta^2b^2\right\}
 \lesssim T,
\]
because \(T\le1\) eventually.  Thus in both cases there is an admissible pair with objective at most a constant multiple of \(T\).  Combining this fact with (5) and (6) proves
\[
 \inf_{\substack{h\le r_0,\ 1\le k\le mh^d\\ mh^d\ge C_S^2\log(8/\eta)}}
 \{B(h,k)+S(h,k,\eta)\}
 \asymp r_{\mathrm{np}}\vee n^{-q/d}.
\]
The final assertion follows immediately: the right-hand side is comparable to \(r_{\mathrm{np}}\) exactly when \(r_{\mathrm{np}}\gtrsim n^{-q/d}\), whereas in the reverse regime the rank constraint produces the additional \(n^{-q/d}\) floor established in (2).
